docs.title: PinGoblin ADS1115 ADC Breakout
docs.text:
The ADS1115 breakout adds four 16-bit analogue inputs to a Raspberry Pi, ESP32 or any other I²C host. Each channel has its own 3-pin sensor header, a protected input and a solder jumper that sets it up for bare resistive sensors. This site is the documentation for the board and its software.

  • User guide

    Setting up and using the board: pinouts and dimensions, wiring, connecting sensors, configuration, accuracy and calibration, specifications, safety and troubleshooting.

  • API

    The Raspberry Pi and MicroPython modules: installation, example scripts and the full function reference.

docs.title: ADS1115 API
docs.text:
The repository has one library for each kind of host, with the same methods on both, and example scripts for each.

Folder Runs on What it is Dependencies python/ Raspberry Pi and other Linux boards pingoblin_ads1115 package, which talks to the chip directly, and six example scripts smbus2, installed automatically micropython/ ESP32, Raspberry Pi Pico and other MicroPython boards ads1115 module, which talks to the chip directly, and two example scripts None

docs.title: Raspberry Pi quick start
docs.text:
Enable I²C with sudo raspi-config (Interface Options → I2C), reboot, then:

i2cdetect -y 1           # the board should appear at 48 (or 49/4a/4b)
python3 -m venv ~/ads-env && source ~/ads-env/bin/activate
pip install "git+https://github.com/PinGoblin/ADS1115#subdirectory=python"

Then, in your own code:

from pingoblin_ads1115 import ADS1115, resistance_from_voltage, ntc_celsius

adc = ADS1115(address=0x48)                 # I²C bus 1, ±4.096 V, 128 samples/s
v = adc.read_voltage(0, samples=16)         # CH0 (J2), volts
print(ntc_celsius(resistance_from_voltage(v, vdd=3.30)))   # with JP5 (RES) closed

To run the examples, copy the python folder to the Pi and run python3 01_read_all_channels.py inside it.

The Raspberry Pi library is thread-safe: several threads can share one board, because only one conversion runs at a time. The PinGoblin DRV8874 motor driver library uses it to read motor current.

docs.title: MicroPython quick start
docs.text:
Copy ads1115.py to the board with Thonny or mpremote cp ads1115.py :, or install it with mpremote mip install github:PinGoblin/ADS1115/micropython, then:

from machine import I2C, Pin
from ads1115 import ADS1115

i2c = I2C(0, scl=Pin(22), sda=Pin(21), freq=100_000)   # ESP32 defaults
adc = ADS1115(i2c, address=0x48, fsr=4.096, rate=128)
print([adc.read_voltage(ch) for ch in range(4)])

docs.title: Choosing settings
docs.text:
Both libraries take the same arguments:

Setting Argument Recommended I²C address address=0x48 Match the board's address jumper Full-scale range fsr=4.096 ±4.096 V on a 3.3 V board Samples per second rate=128 128; 8 for calibration and slow sensors I²C bus (Raspberry Pi only) bus=1 1, the Pi's header I²C bus

See Configuration for the full range table and Accuracy and calibration for calibration.

docs.title: Conversion formulas
docs.text:
Vadc is the voltage the ADC reports. For a resistive sensor with the RES jumper closed, the sensor's resistance is (resistance_from_voltage()):

Rs = 10 kΩ × Vadc / (VDD − Vadc)

For an NTC thermistor, temperature in kelvin follows from the Beta equation (ntc_celsius()), using R0, T0 and B from the thermistor's datasheet (commonly 10 kΩ, 298.15 K and 3950):

1/T = 1/T0 + ln(Rs / R0) / B

Subtract 273.15 to convert kelvin to degrees Celsius. For voltage-output sensors, use the sensor's own datasheet formula on Vadc directly.

docs.title: main.py
docs.text:
micropython/main.py
"""ESP32 MicroPython example: a thermistor on CH0 and voltages on CH1–CH3.

Prints the temperature and three voltages once a second. Copy `ads1115.py` and this
file to the ESP32, then reset it.

**Wiring** (ESP32 DevKit defaults; change the pins below for other boards)

| Breakout J1 | ESP32 |
|---|---|
| VDD | 3V3 |
| GND | GND |
| SCL | GPIO22 |
| SDA | GPIO21 |

**Board setup**

- CH0 (J2): 10 kΩ NTC thermistor on the SIG and GND pins, RES jumper JP5 closed.
- CH1–CH3 (J3–J5): voltage-output sensors, RES open.
"""
import math
import time
from machine import I2C, Pin

from ads1115 import ADS1115

VDD = 3.30            # measure your board's real VDD (TP5 to TP6)
R_EXC = 10_000        # excitation resistor fitted on the board
R0, T0_C, BETA = 10_000, 25.0, 3950   # thermistor datasheet values
R_OPEN = 5_000_000    # above this the thermistor is treated as disconnected

# 100 kHz suits the board's 10 kΩ pull-ups; use 400 kHz only with 2.2-4.7 kΩ pull-ups added
i2c = I2C(0, scl=Pin(22), sda=Pin(21), freq=100_000)
found = i2c.scan()
print("I2C devices:", [hex(a) for a in found])
if 0x48 not in found:
    raise SystemExit("ADS1115 not found at 0x48 - check wiring and the address jumpers")

adc = ADS1115(i2c, address=0x48, fsr=4.096, rate=128)


def ntc_celsius(v):
    """Convert the CH0 voltage to °C (Beta equation), or `None` for an open or short circuit."""
    if v <= 0 or v >= VDD:
        return None
    r = R_EXC * v / (VDD - v)
    if r > R_OPEN:
        return None
    return 1 / (1 / (T0_C + 273.15) + math.log(r / R0) / BETA) - 273.15


while True:
    v = [adc.read_voltage(0, samples=4)]
    if adc.clipped:
        print("CH0 at full scale: on a 5 V board use fsr=6.144")
    v += [adc.read_voltage(ch, samples=4) for ch in (1, 2, 3)]
    t = ntc_celsius(v[0])
    t_txt = "--.-" if t is None else "%.2f" % t
    print("T=%s C   CH1=%.3f V  CH2=%.3f V  CH3=%.3f V" % (t_txt, v[1], v[2], v[3]))
    time.sleep(1)

docs.title: ready_pin_fast.py
docs.text:
micropython/ready_pin_fast.py
"""ESP32 MicroPython example: fast sampling with the RDY pin.

Instead of waiting a fixed time, the ADS1115 pulls RDY low the moment each conversion
finishes, and the ESP32 catches that edge with an interrupt. Samples CH0 at the 860 samples/s
data rate for 2 seconds and prints the statistics. Reading each result over I²C adds time, so
the achieved rate is lower at 100 kHz; add 2.2–4.7 kΩ pull-ups from SDA and SCL to 3.3 V and
set `freq=400_000` to get closer to 860.

**Extra wiring:** breakout J1 pin 5 (RDY) to ESP32 GPIO4. The board already has a
10 kΩ pull-up on RDY.

Run with `mpremote run ready_pin_fast.py`.
"""
import time
from machine import I2C, Pin

from ads1115 import ADS1115

i2c = I2C(0, scl=Pin(22), sda=Pin(21), freq=100_000)
adc = ADS1115(i2c, fsr=4.096, rate=860)
adc.enable_ready_pin()

ready = False


def on_ready(pin):
    """Interrupt handler: flag that a conversion has finished."""
    global ready
    ready = True


rdy = Pin(4, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP)
rdy.irq(trigger=Pin.IRQ_FALLING, handler=on_ready)

samples = []
deadline = time.ticks_add(time.ticks_ms(), 2000)
adc.start(0)
while time.ticks_diff(deadline, time.ticks_ms()) > 0:
    if ready:
        ready = False
        samples.append(adc.result_voltage())
        adc.start(0)

n = len(samples)
if n:
    mean = sum(samples) / n
    print("%d samples in 2 s (%.0f per s)" % (n, n / 2))
    print("mean %.4f V  min %.4f V  max %.4f V" % (mean, min(samples), max(samples)))
else:
    print("No ready pulses - check the RDY wire to GPIO4")

docs.title: 01_read_all_channels.py
docs.text:
python/01_read_all_channels.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Example 1: read all four channels.

Prints the raw count and voltage of CH0–CH3 twice a second. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

**Board setup**

- Host on J1.
- Voltage-output sensors on J2–J5 (GND, VDD, SIG).
- All RES jumpers open (the factory default).

Applies the calibration from `06_calibrate.py` if `calibration.json` exists.
"""
import time

from pingoblin_ads1115 import ADS1115, load_calibration, apply_calibration

adc = ADS1115(address=0x48, fsr=4.096)         # +/-4.096 V full scale, 128 samples/s
cal = load_calibration()                       # optional, see 06_calibrate.py

print("CH0 (J2)        CH1 (J3)        CH2 (J4)        CH3 (J5)")
try:
    while True:
        cells = []
        for ch in range(4):
            raw = adc.read_raw(ch)
            volts = apply_calibration(raw * adc.fsr / 32768, ch, cal)
            cells.append(f"{raw:6d} {volts:6.3f}V")
        print("  ".join(cells))
        time.sleep(0.5)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

docs.title: 02_thermistor_ntc.py
docs.text:
python/02_thermistor_ntc.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Example 2: temperature from a 10 kΩ NTC thermistor.

**Board setup**

- Close the RES jumper of the channel you use (JP5 for CH0).
- Connect one thermistor lead to SIG (pin 3) and the other to GND (pin 1) of J2.
  The VDD pin is not used, and a thermistor has no polarity.

**Accuracy tips**

- Measure the board's real VDD between TP5 and TP6 and set `VDD`, or
- set `VDD_CHANNEL` to a spare channel and link that header's VDD pin to its SIG pin with
  a jumper wire (RES open). The script then measures VDD live.
- Set `R0`, `T0_C` and `BETA` from your thermistor's datasheet.
"""
import time

from pingoblin_ads1115 import (ADS1115, resistance_from_voltage, ntc_celsius,
                               load_calibration, apply_calibration)

NTC_CHANNEL = 0        # CH0 = J2, RES jumper JP5 closed
VDD = 3.30             # your measured supply voltage
VDD_CHANNEL = None     # e.g. 3 to measure VDD live on CH3 (J5 VDD linked to SIG)

# Thermistor datasheet values
R0 = 10_000.0          # resistance at T0
T0_C = 25.0
BETA = 3950.0          # check your part: 3380, 3435 and 3950 are all common

R_OPEN = 5_000_000     # above this the thermistor is treated as disconnected (a 10 k NTC is ~1 M at -55 C)

adc = ADS1115(fsr=4.096)
cal = load_calibration()

try:
    while True:
        vdd = VDD
        if VDD_CHANNEL is not None:
            vdd = apply_calibration(adc.read_voltage(VDD_CHANNEL, samples=8), VDD_CHANNEL, cal)
        v = apply_calibration(adc.read_voltage(NTC_CHANNEL, samples=16), NTC_CHANNEL, cal)
        if adc.clipped:
            print("Reading at full scale: on a 5 V board use ADS1115(fsr=6.144)")
        r = resistance_from_voltage(v, vdd)
        if r > R_OPEN:
            print("Open circuit - is the thermistor connected and RES closed?")
        elif r < 50:
            print("Short circuit - check the thermistor wiring")
        else:
            t = ntc_celsius(r, R0, T0_C, BETA)
            print(f"V={v:.4f} V  VDD={vdd:.3f} V  R={r/1000:7.3f} k  T={t:6.2f} C")
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

docs.title: 03_light_and_pot.py
docs.text:
python/03_light_and_pot.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Example 3: two sensor types on one board.

Shows how a voltage-output channel and a resistive channel are converted differently.

**Board setup**

| Channel | Sensor | RES jumper | Wiring |
|---|---|---|---|
| CH0 (J2) | Potentiometer | Open | Ends to GND and VDD, wiper to SIG |
| CH1 (J3) | Bare LDR | Closed (JP6) | One lead to SIG, the other to GND |
"""
import time

from pingoblin_ads1115 import ADS1115, resistance_from_voltage, percent_of_range

VDD = 3.30

adc = ADS1115(fsr=4.096)
POT, LDR = 0, 1        # channels

try:
    while True:
        v_pot = adc.read_voltage(POT, samples=8)
        pot_pct = percent_of_range(v_pot, 0.0, VDD)

        v_ldr = adc.read_voltage(LDR, samples=8)
        r_ldr = resistance_from_voltage(v_ldr, VDD)
        # LDR resistance falls as light rises; dark ~1 M, bright ~1 k.
        # Brightness is shown as % of the voltage swing (bright = low voltage).
        light_pct = 100.0 - percent_of_range(v_ldr, 0.0, VDD)

        r_txt = "open" if r_ldr == float("inf") else f"{r_ldr/1000:8.1f} k"
        print(f"Pot {pot_pct:5.1f} %   |   LDR {r_txt}  light {light_pct:5.1f} %")
        time.sleep(0.25)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

docs.title: 04_multiple_boards.py
docs.text:
python/04_multiple_boards.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Example 4: several boards on one I²C bus, up to 16 channels.

Finds every board at 0x48–0x4B and prints all their channels once a second.

**Board setup**

Give every board a different address with the solder jumpers:

| Board | Jumpers | Address |
|---|---|---|
| A | JP1 closed (default) | 0x48 |
| B | Cut JP1, close JP2 | 0x49 |
| C | Cut JP1, close JP3 | 0x4A |
| D | Cut JP1, close JP4 | 0x4B |

Wire pins 1–4 of every board's J1 (VDD, GND, SCL, SDA) in parallel to the Pi.
`i2cdetect -y 1` lists the addresses the Pi can see. Up to four boards can share the Pi's bus.
"""
import time

from pingoblin_ads1115 import find_boards

boards = find_boards(fsr=4.096)          # tries 0x48-0x4B on I2C bus 1
for addr in boards:
    print(f"Found board at 0x{addr:02X}")

if not boards:
    raise SystemExit("No boards found - check wiring, power and `i2cdetect -y 1`.")

try:
    while True:
        line = []
        for addr, adc in boards.items():
            volts = " ".join(f"{adc.read_voltage(ch):5.3f}" for ch in range(4))
            line.append(f"0x{addr:02X}: {volts}")
        print("  |  ".join(line))
        time.sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass

docs.text:
python/05_csv_logger.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Example 5: log all four channels to a CSV file.

Each row holds an ISO timestamp, then CH0–CH3 in volts (16-sample averages). Open the file
in a spreadsheet to chart it. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

**Usage**

```bash
python3 05_csv_logger.py                 # every 5 s to ads_log.csv
python3 05_csv_logger.py 60 garden.csv   # every 60 s to garden.csv
""" import csv import os import sys import time from datetime import datetime

from pingoblin_ads1115 import ADS1115, load_calibration, apply_calibration

interval = float(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 5.0 path = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else "ads_log.csv"

adc = ADS1115(fsr=4.096, rate=128) cal = load_calibration()

new_file = not os.path.exists(path) with open(path, "a", newline="") as f: writer = csv.writer(f) if new_file: writer.writerow(["timestamp", "ch0_V", "ch1_V", "ch2_V", "ch3_V"]) print(f"Logging every {interval:g} s to {path} - Ctrl+C to stop") try: while True: start = time.monotonic() row = [datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="seconds")] for ch in range(4): row.append(f"{apply_calibration(adc.read_voltage(ch, samples=16), ch, cal):.5f}") writer.writerow(row) f.flush() print(", ".join(row)) time.sleep(max(0.0, interval - (time.monotonic() - start))) except KeyboardInterrupt: pass

## 06_calibrate.py

```python title="python/06_calibrate.py"
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Example 6: one-point gain calibration.

Removes the small gain error caused by the 4.7 kΩ series resistor and the ADC's own
tolerance (typically 0.1–0.2 %).

1. Leave the channel's RES jumper open.
2. Link the header's VDD pin to its SIG pin with a jumper wire, or apply any steady
   voltage between 1 V and VDD.
3. Measure that voltage at the header with a good multimeter.
4. Run `python3 06_calibrate.py <channel> <multimeter volts>`,
   for example `python3 06_calibrate.py 0 3.297`.

The factor is saved to `calibration.json` and applied automatically by the other
examples. Repeat for each channel you use.
"""
import sys

from pingoblin_ads1115 import ADS1115, load_calibration, save_calibration

if len(sys.argv) != 3:
    raise SystemExit(__doc__)

ch = int(sys.argv[1])
true_v = float(sys.argv[2])
if ch not in range(4) or not 0.5 <= true_v <= 5.5:
    raise SystemExit("Channel must be 0-3 and voltage 0.5-5.5 V")

adc = ADS1115(fsr=4.096, rate=8)           # slowest rate = lowest noise
measured = adc.read_voltage(ch, samples=32)
if measured < 0.25:
    raise SystemExit(f"CH{ch} reads {measured:.4f} V - is the voltage connected?")

factor = true_v / measured
if not 0.97 <= factor <= 1.03:
    raise SystemExit(f"Factor {factor:.5f} is outside +/-3 % - check the wiring and meter")

cal = load_calibration()
cal[str(ch)] = round(factor, 6)
save_calibration(cal)
print(f"CH{ch}: measured {measured:.5f} V, true {true_v:.5f} V -> factor {factor:.5f} saved")

docs.title: MicroPython module: ads1115
docs.text:
MicroPython module for the PinGoblin ADS1115 4-channel ADC breakout.

Runs on the ESP32, Raspberry Pi Pico and any other MicroPython board with machine.I2C. It has no dependencies: copy this file to the board with Thonny or mpremote cp ads1115.py :.

Each read starts a single-shot conversion, waits for it to finish and returns the result. For faster sampling, use start() with the RDY pin (see ready_pin_fast.py).

Example 
from machine import I2C, Pin
from ads1115 import ADS1115

i2c = I2C(0, scl=Pin(22), sda=Pin(21), freq=100_000)   # ESP32 defaults
adc = ADS1115(i2c)                  # address 0x48, ±4.096 V, 128 samples/s
print(adc.read_voltage(0))          # CH0 (header J2), volts

docs.title: ADS1115
docs.text:
ADS1115(
    i2c,
    address: int = 72,
    fsr: float = 4.096,
    rate: int = 128,
)

One ADS1115 breakout on an I²C bus.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default i2c I2C

A machine.I2C (or SoftI2C) object. Use 100 kHz with only the board's 10 kΩ pull-ups; 400 kHz needs 2.2–4.7 kΩ pull-ups to 3.3 V at the host.

required address int

I²C address set by the address jumpers: 0x48 (default), 0x49, 0x4A or 0x4B.

72 fsr float

Full-scale range (±V): 6.144, 4.096, 2.048, 1.024, 0.512 or 0.256. Use 4.096 on a 3.3 V board.

4.096 rate int

Samples per second: 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 250, 475 or 860.

128

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If address, fsr or rate is not one of the allowed values.

Attributes:

Name Type Description i2c

The I²C bus.

address int

The board's I²C address.

fsr float

Full-scale range (±V). Can be changed between reads.

rate int

Samples per second. Can be changed between reads.

clipped bool

True if any conversion in the most recent read hit full scale (±fsr), so the input may be beyond the range. Use a larger fsr if it is.

docs.title: enable_ready_pin
docs.text:
enable_ready_pin() -> None

Make the RDY pin pulse low each time a conversion finishes.

RDY is J1 pin 5 (the chip's ALERT/RDY pin), pulled up to VDD on the board. Wire it to a GPIO and trigger an interrupt on the falling edge. Each board needs its own GPIO.

docs.text:
start(channel: int) -> None

Start a conversion and return at once, without waiting for the result.

Read the result with result_voltage() after the RDY pin pulses (see enable_ready_pin()), or after 1/rate seconds.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default channel int

Channel number, 0 to 3.

required

docs.title: Raspberry Pi package: pingoblin_ads1115
docs.text:
Raspberry Pi library for the PinGoblin ADS1115 4-channel 16-bit ADC board.

Talks to the ADS1115 directly with smbus2, and has the same methods as the MicroPython ads1115 module. It also works with any other ADS1115 breakout.

Install on the Pi, in a virtual environment:

pip install "git+https://github.com/PinGoblin/ADS1115#subdirectory=python"
Name Purpose ADS1115 One board: single-ended and differential reads, range, data rate, RDY pin find_boards() Finds every board on the bus (0x48–0x4B) resistance_from_voltage() Resistive sensor resistance with the RES jumper closed ntc_celsius() Thermistor temperature (Beta equation) percent_of_range() Voltage as a percentage of a range load_calibration(), apply_calibration(), save_calibration() Per-channel gain correction

docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
This board adds four 16-bit analogue inputs to a Raspberry Pi, ESP32 or any other I²C host, and is built to survive wiring mistakes. It uses the Texas Instruments ADS1115 ADC. PinGoblin's Raspberry Pi and MicroPython libraries drive it directly, and it also works with other ADS1115 libraries.

This user guide covers the board hardware: pinouts, wiring, sensors, configuration, accuracy, specifications and troubleshooting. The Python and MicroPython code is described in the API section.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• 4 single-ended inputs (or 2 differential pairs), 16-bit, up to 860 samples per second
  • Plug-and-play sensor headers: one 3-pin header (GND, VDD, SIG) per channel
  • Protected inputs: a 4.7 kΩ series resistor on every channel survives an accidental connection to ±15 V
  • Resistive sensors without extra parts: close a channel's RES jumper to connect a bare thermistor, LDR or force sensor
  • One 2.54 mm header for the host (VDD, GND, SCL, SDA, RDY)
  • Four I²C addresses: up to four boards (16 channels) on one bus
  • Test pads on every input and bus signal, and four M2.5 mounting holes
  • Under 5 µA when idle: no power LED, so it suits battery-powered projects
  • Nothing to fit or remove: every component is factory-fitted; options are set with solder jumpers

docs.title: Summary specifications
docs.text:
Specification Value ADC TI ADS1115, 16-bit delta-sigma, internal reference Channels 4 single-ended or 2 differential Sample rate 8 to 860 samples/s (programmable) Programmable gain ranges ±6.144, ±4.096, ±2.048, ±1.024, ±0.512, ±0.256 V Supply voltage (VDD) 2.7 to 5.25 V (use 3.3 V with a Raspberry Pi or ESP32) Supply current Under 5 µA idle, 300 µA max while converting (sensors not included) Sensor supply (VDD on J2–J5) 500 mA max, all headers combined (and within your host's 3.3 V supply) Input voltage range 0 V to VDD Interface I²C, addresses 0x48 (default), 0x49, 0x4A, 0x4B Input series resistor 4.7 kΩ, 1 % Input filter 100 nF per channel (about 340 Hz corner with 4.7 kΩ) Resistive-sensor excitation 10 kΩ to VDD, enabled per channel by the RES jumper On-board I²C pull-ups 10 kΩ on SDA, SCL and RDY

Full limits are in Electrical specifications and safety.

docs.title: Accuracy and calibration
docs.text:
Uncalibrated, expect about ±0.3 % of reading on voltage inputs; a one-point calibration brings this close to the ADC's own limit. For resistive sensors, knowing the real VDD matters more than anything else.

Error source Typical size How to reduce it 4.7 kΩ series resistor against the ADC's input impedance About 0.1 % low at ±4.096 V; up to about 0.7 % at ±0.256 V One-point calibration (06_calibrate.py) ADS1115 gain and offset error About 0.01 % typical, 0.15 % maximum One-point calibration Unknown VDD (resistive sensors only) 1 % VDD error gives about 0.3–0.5 °C on a 10 k NTC at room temperature Measure VDD at TP5–TP6, or measure it live on a spare channel 10 kΩ excitation resistor tolerance (1 %) About 0.25 °C on a 10 k NTC Calibrate against a reference thermometer Thermistor tolerance and Beta value ±0.2 to ±1 °C, depending on the part Use the exact datasheet Beta value or a Steinhart–Hart fit Noise A few counts at 128 samples/s Average readings, or lower the data rate

docs.title: One-point voltage calibration
docs.text:
1. Leave the channel's RES jumper open.
  2. Link the channel header's VDD pin to its SIG pin with a jumper wire.
  3. Measure the voltage at that header with a good multimeter.
  4. Run python3 06_calibrate.py <channel> <volts>, for example python3 06_calibrate.py 0 3.297.
  5. Repeat for each channel. The examples apply the stored factors automatically.

docs.title: Measuring VDD live
docs.text: Link a spare channel's VDD pin to its SIG pin (RES open) and set VDD_CHANNEL in 02_thermistor_ntc.py. The script then uses the measured supply for every reading, which also tracks supply drift.

docs.title: Temperature calibration
docs.text: For the best thermistor accuracy, place the thermistor next to a trusted thermometer at a temperature in the middle of your range and adjust BETA or R0 until the readings agree.

docs.title: Board layout and pinouts
docs.text: The host connects to J1, and each sensor gets its own 3-pin header.

docs.title: J1 — host header (1×5, 2.54 mm)
docs.text: Pin Signal Connect to 1 VDD 3.3 V supply from the host (2.7–5.25 V allowed) 2 GND Host ground 3 SCL I²C clock 4 SDA I²C data 5 RDY (the ADC's ALERT/RDY pin) Optional: a GPIO input for conversion-ready or threshold alerts

docs.title: J2–J5 — sensor headers (1×3, 2.54 mm, one per channel)
docs.text:
Header Channel Pin 1 Pin 2 Pin 3 J2 CH0 (A0) GND VDD SIG J3 CH1 (A1) GND VDD SIG J4 CH2 (A2) GND VDD SIG J5 CH3 (A3) GND VDD SIG

VDD on the sensor headers is a supply output

It is the board's own supply (whatever J1 provides) and is there to power the sensor. Never connect an external supply to it: a 5 V sensor's supply goes to your 5 V source, and only its GND and SIG go to the header. Keep the total load across all four headers to 500 mA or less, and within what your host's 3.3 V supply can provide. That is plenty for sensor modules, but not for motors, relays or gas-sensor heaters.

docs.title: Solder jumpers
docs.text: Jumper Default Function JP1 Closed (trace) I²C address 0x48 (ADDR to GND through a 10 kΩ resistor, R13) JP2 Open I²C address 0x49 (ADDR to VDD) JP3 Open I²C address 0x4A (ADDR to SDA) JP4 Open I²C address 0x4B (ADDR to SCL) JP5–JP8 (RES) Open Close to enable the 10 kΩ excitation resistor on CH0–CH3 for resistive sensors

docs.title: Test pads and other parts
docs.text:
Test pads (1.5 mm): TP1–TP4 on the ADC side of each input (AIN0–AIN3), TP5 VDD, TP6 GND, TP7 SDA, TP8 SCL, TP9 RDY.

Other: H1–H4 M2.5 mounting holes (2.7 mm, unplated, not connected). There is no power LED, which keeps the idle current under 5 µA: to check the board is powered, measure TP5 to TP6 or run an I²C scan.

docs.title: Dimensions
docs.text: Top view. All dimensions in mm, from the left edge (datum A) and bottom edge (datum B) to feature centres.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Three things can be configured: the I²C address and each channel's RES mode, set with solder jumpers, and the full-scale range and data rate, set in software.

Working with solder jumpers. To close a jumper, heat both pads with a soldering iron and add a small blob of solder so it bridges them. To open JP1, cut the thin copper trace between its pads with a sharp craft knife, then check with a multimeter that the pads are no longer connected. Re-solder JP1 to restore the default.

I²C address. Exactly one address jumper must be closed. If you close JP2 and forget to cut JP1, nothing is damaged (JP1 connects through a 10 kΩ resistor) and the board answers at 0x49, but JP1 must be cut for 0x4A and 0x4B or the bus stops working.

Address JP1 (GND) JP2 (VDD) JP3 (SDA) JP4 (SCL) 0x48 (default) Closed Open Open Open 0x49 Cut Closed Open Open 0x4A Cut Open Closed Open 0x4B Cut Open Open Closed

When you set up several boards, use the addresses in the order 0x48, 0x49, 0x4B and then 0x4A. Address 0x4A connects ADDR to SDA, which relies on the host holding SDA steady for 100 ns after each clock edge; TI recommends using it last.

Using several boards. Give each board a different address and wire their J1 pins 1–4 (VDD, GND, SCL, SDA) in parallel. Example 04_multiple_boards.py finds and reads all of them. To use the RDY signal, wire each board's J1 pin 5 to its own GPIO (the examples poll instead, so RDY is optional).

Bus pull-ups and speed. Each board adds 10 kΩ pull-ups on SDA and SCL. With a Raspberry Pi (1.8 kΩ on board), the bus can take four 10 kΩ pull-up pairs in total: four of these boards, or fewer boards plus other devices that have their own 10 kΩ pull-ups. More than that overloads the bus, which must be able to pull it low with 3 mA. With only the board's own pull-ups, as on an ESP32, run the bus at 100 kHz (the MicroPython examples do). For 400 kHz, add 2.2–4.7 kΩ resistors from SDA and SCL to 3.3 V at the host.

RES jumpers. JP5–JP8 enable the 10 kΩ excitation resistor for CH0–CH3. Leave them open for voltage-output sensors; close them only for bare resistive sensors (see Connecting sensors).

Full-scale range (programmable gain). Set in software with fsr= when you create the ADS1115 object (Raspberry Pi and MicroPython alike), or change adc.fsr between reads. Choose the smallest range that still covers your highest expected voltage.

fsr Full-scale range Resolution (1 count) Use for 6.144 ±6.144 V 187.5 µV Boards powered at 5 V, including RES-mode channels 4.096 (recommended) ±4.096 V 125 µV Anything up to 3.3 V 2.048 ±2.048 V 62.5 µV Signals below 2 V 1.024 ±1.024 V 31.3 µV Signals below 1 V 0.512 ±0.512 V 15.6 µV Small signals, differential pairs 0.256 ±0.256 V 7.8 µV Very small differential signals

The full-scale range never lets an input exceed VDD: on a 3.3 V board, the ±6.144 V and ±4.096 V settings both still read 0–3.3 V.

A reading above the full-scale range stops at full scale. After each read, adc.clipped is True if any conversion hit full scale. On a 5 V board with fsr=4.096, a resistive sensor above about 45 kΩ (a 10 kΩ thermistor colder than about −5 °C) clips, so use fsr=6.144 there.

Data rate. Set with rate= or adc.rate (8 to 860 samples/s). Slower rates give lower noise; 128 samples/s is a good default, and 8 samples/s is best for calibration and slow sensors such as temperature.

Differential inputs. Pairs CH0–CH1, CH0–CH3, CH1–CH3 and CH2–CH3 can be read differentially, for example across a current-sense resistor. Both inputs must stay between GND and VDD, and both channels' RES jumpers must be open.

docs.title: Connecting sensors
docs.text:
Most sensors plug straight into a channel header with the factory settings; only bare resistive sensors need the channel's RES jumper closed. Choose the row that matches your sensor.

Sensor type Examples RES jumper Header pins used Reading Voltage-output module (3 wires) Analogue sensor modules, TMP36, capacitive soil probes, joysticks, Hall sensors Open (default) GND, VDD, SIG Vin = Vadc Potentiometer Knobs, sliders Open (default) Ends to GND and VDD, wiper to SIG % = Vadc / VDD × 100 Bare resistive sensor (2 wires) 10 k NTC thermistor, LDR, force-sensitive resistor, flex sensor Closed SIG and GND only Rs = 10 kΩ × Vadc / (VDD − Vadc) 5 V sensor MQ gas modules, 0.5–4.5 V pressure transducers Open (default) GND and SIG only; power the sensor from 5 V separately See below

Voltage-output sensors. Plug the sensor's 3-pin cable into the channel header, matching the GND, VDD and SIG labels on the silkscreen to the sensor's ground, supply and signal wires. Check the sensor works at 3.3 V; many maker modules accept 3.3–5 V.

Resistive sensors. Close the channel's RES jumper (JP5 for CH0, JP6 for CH1, JP7 for CH2, JP8 for CH3) with a small blob of solder. Connect one sensor lead to SIG and the other to GND; there is no polarity. The on-board 10 kΩ resistor and the sensor then form a voltage divider. Choose sensors whose resistance is roughly 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ over your range for best resolution; a 10 kΩ sensor gives the most resolution near its nominal value.

5 V sensors. Power the sensor from a separate 5 V supply (for example the Raspberry Pi's 5 V pin), connect its ground to the header's GND pin and its output to SIG. The sensor's output must stay below the board's VDD + 0.3 V (3.6 V on a 3.3 V board). If it can go higher, add a resistor divider on the sensor side; the 4.7 kΩ series resistor protects the ADC from brief mistakes but is not a level shifter.

Cable runs. Leads of a few metres are fine; use twisted or shielded cable for longer runs and keep it away from mains and motor wiring. The 100 nF filter on each channel removes most interference.

Not supported on this board. Industrial 0–10 V and 4–20 mA signals, thermocouples, RTDs (PT100/PT1000), load cells and digital sensors (DHT22, DS18B20, I²C sensors). Thermocouples, RTDs and load cells need dedicated amplifier boards; digital sensors connect to the host directly.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Power the board from 3.3 V, connect four wires, install the library and run the first example. The board appears at I²C address 0x48 out of the box.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi wiring (J1)
docs.text: Breakout J1 Raspberry Pi header 1 VDD Pin 1 (3V3) 2 GND Pin 6 (GND) 3 SCL Pin 5 (GPIO3 / SCL) 4 SDA Pin 3 (GPIO2 / SDA) 5 RDY Optional: any free GPIO

docs.title: ESP32 DevKit wiring (J1)
docs.text: VDD to 3V3, GND to GND, SCL to GPIO22, SDA to GPIO21.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi software
docs.text:
1. Enable I²C: sudo raspi-config → Interface Options → I2C → Enable, then reboot.
  2. Check the board is seen: i2cdetect -y 1 should show 48.
  3. Install the library in a virtual environment:
    1. python3 -m venv ~/ads-env
    2. source ~/ads-env/bin/activate
    3. pip install "git+https://github.com/PinGoblin/ADS1115#subdirectory=python"
  4. Copy the python folder from the repository to the Pi and run python3 01_read_all_channels.py inside it.

docs.title: ESP32 software (MicroPython)
docs.text:
1. Flash MicroPython onto the ESP32.
  2. Copy ads1115.py and main.py from the micropython folder to the board with Thonny or mpremote cp.
  3. Reset the board; readings print once a second.

Note

With nothing connected, the inputs float and show random values; this is normal.

docs.title: Electrical specifications and safety
docs.text: Run the board from 2.7–5.25 V and keep every input between 0 V and VDD; the protection is for mistakes, not for continuous use outside these limits.

docs.title: Operating conditions
docs.text: Parameter Min Typical Max Unit Supply voltage, VDD 2.7 3.3 5.25 V Supply current, board only, idle (ADC powered down between readings) — 0.5 5 µA Supply current, board only, while converting — 150 300 µA Sensor supply current, VDD on J2–J5, all headers combined — — 500 mA Extra current per channel with RES closed — — 0.33 mA (at 3.3 V) Input voltage for valid readings 0 — VDD V Sample rate 8 128 860 samples/s I²C clock, using only the board's 10 kΩ pull-ups (e.g. ESP32) — 100 100 kHz I²C clock with 2.2–4.7 kΩ host pull-ups (the Raspberry Pi has 1.8 kΩ) — 100 / 400 400 kHz Operating temperature −40 — 85 °C

docs.title: Absolute maximum ratings
docs.text:
Exceeding these may damage the board.

Parameter Limit VDD −0.3 V to 5.5 V Brief fault voltage on a sensor SIG pin (series resistor protection) −15 V to +15 V Continuous voltage on a sensor SIG pin −0.3 V to VDD + 0.3 V Voltage on I²C and RDY pins −0.3 V to 5.5 V

The ADS1115 itself runs from 2.0 V, but below 2.7 V the I²C logic margins are small and no Raspberry Pi or ESP32 runs its bus that low. VDD is limited to 5.5 V (not the chip's 7 V) because the on-board pull-ups connect SDA, SCL and RDY to VDD, and those pins are rated to 5.5 V.

docs.title: Safety and handling
docs.text:
• This is a low-voltage board. Never connect it to mains voltage or to circuits referenced to mains.
  • The I²C pull-ups connect to VDD, so the bus runs at the board's supply voltage. Power the board from 3.3 V when it is wired to a Raspberry Pi or an ESP32: their I²C pins are not 5 V tolerant.
  • A fault voltage on an input pushes up to about 4 mA per channel into the board's supply. A brief mistake is harmless when the board runs from a Raspberry Pi or ESP32 3.3 V pin, because the host's own load absorbs it. A supply with very little other load (for example a small regulator powering only this board) cannot absorb it, and its voltage can rise. Fix the wiring before leaving the board powered.
  • Connect and disconnect J1 with the power off.
  • The board is static-sensitive: handle it by the edges and avoid touching the inputs while unpowered sensors are being connected.
  • Disconnect power before closing or cutting solder jumpers.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Most problems come down to I²C wiring, a jumper in the wrong state or a floating input; work through the table from the top.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Board not found, and TP5 to TP6 reads 0 V No supply on VDD, or VDD and GND swapped (the board has no power LED) Check J1 pins 1 and 2 i2cdetect shows nothing I²C disabled, SDA and SCL swapped, or no common ground Enable I²C in raspi-config; check pins 3 and 5 on the Pi; check GND Board appears at an unexpected address Address jumpers changed Check JP1–JP4; exactly one must be closed No address appears after setting 0x4A or 0x4B JP1 not fully cut, so SDA or SCL is held low Re-cut JP1 and check it with a multimeter Board still at 0x49 after closing JP3 or JP4 JP2 is still closed Remove the solder from JP2 ESP32 I²C errors or missing devices at 400 kHz Only the board's 10 kΩ pull-ups on the bus, so the edges are too slow Use freq=100_000, or add 2.2–4.7 kΩ pull-ups to 3.3 V Readings jump around with nothing connected Input is floating (normal) Connect a sensor, or close the RES jumper to pull the input to VDD Channel reads close to VDD all the time RES closed with an open-circuit sensor, or a broken sensor wire Check the sensor and its wiring; open RES if the sensor outputs a voltage Voltage sensor reads too high or wrong RES jumper closed on a voltage-output channel Open the RES jumper (remove the solder bridge with solder wick) Thermistor temperature a few degrees out Wrong Beta value or wrong VDD in the script Use the datasheet Beta; measure VDD (see Accuracy and calibration) Readings stop at about 3.3 V Input is at VDD; the ADC cannot read above its supply Keep inputs below VDD; divide higher voltages before the board Readings stop at 4.096 V on a 5 V board (adc.clipped is True) Full-scale range smaller than the input Use fsr=6.144 Very noisy readings Long unshielded leads, or a noisy supply Twist or shield the cable, average readings, lower the data rate ModuleNotFoundError for pingoblin_ads1115 or smbus2 Package missing or wrong virtual environment Activate the environment and run pip install "git+https://github.com/PinGoblin/ADS1115#subdirectory=python" PermissionError or FileNotFoundError for /dev/i2c-1 I²C not enabled, or the user is not in the i2c group Enable I²C with sudo raspi-config, then reboot ESP32 OSError: [Errno 19] ENODEV Wrong pins or address Check SCL = GPIO22 and SDA = GPIO21; run i2c.scan() No ready pulses in ready_pin_fast.py RDY not wired to the interrupt pin Connect J1 pin 5 to GPIO4
